name: Mamvu
catalog_citation: Vorbichler, Anton. 1967. [Review of] A. N. Tucker & M. A. Bryan, Linguistic analyses: the non-Bantu languages of north-eastern Africa (London: OUP, 1966). Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 30(2): 451-452. doi:10.1017/S0041977X00062698 (op…
catalog_locator: p. 452, col. 1, paragraph 'Tone and stress' (a)-(c); page image the copy we hold, scanned the copy we
catalog_quote: Tone and stress. (a) By my analysis of Balese it is now firmly established that three distinctive tonemes exist in Mangbutu-Efe. Since then I have got irrefutable proof for their existence in Mamvu, too. (b) Falling tone in long syllables which are virtually disyllabic, occurs also in Balese. In Efe sometimes the sequence [Falling-High] is a variant for Balese /High-High/, while in Mamvu the sequence /Low-Low/ is realized in slow speech as [Low-Rising]. (c) In Balese a long syllable, not being virtually disyllabic, always indicates a stress on the penultimate of a word, word complex, or syntactic unit. One could regard this length as a juncture chroneme.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mamvu is a tone language with three distinctive level tonemes (High, Mid, Low; a /Low-Low/ sequence may surface as Low-Rising in slow speech). The describer gives no stress-placement rule for Mamvu itself; for the closely related Balese (Lese) he states that stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a word, word complex or syntactic unit and is signalled by vowel length (a 'juncture chroneme').
new_statements.exceptions: None for Mamvu. The penultimate-stress-with-length remark is explicitly restricted to Balese; long syllables that are 'virtually disyllabic' (carrying falling tone) are excluded from it.
new_statements.domain_note: The Balese stress remark ranges over 'word, word complex, or syntactic unit', i.e. it is at least partly phrase-level/junctural; the Mamvu statements concern lexical tonemes. Vorbichler's Mamvu material is from the Mungbere region, checked with a Mamvu informant in 1966; his full treatment of Mamvu tone is Die Sprache der Mamvu (1971) pp. 103-133, not accessible here.
new_statements.identity_note: Vorbichler's Mamvu data are Mamvu proper of the Mungbere/Watsa region (mamv1243, nucl1421 'Nuclear Mamvu'); the only explicit stress-placement clause in the quoted passage concerns Balese (= Lese, ISO les, lese1243), the closest documented relative, not Mamvu. Vorbichler stresses that Mamvu is not mutually intelligible with Balese-Mvuba-Mangbutu-Efe, so the Balese penultimate-stress remark should not be transferred to Mamvu without the 1971 grammar.

new_statements.quote: 2a. Tone. Tone is both lexical and grammatical. In the MORU-MA'DI languages so far investigated (MORU, MA'DI, LOGO, LUGBARA) and in LENDU, three tone levels have been established, and the same would seem to be the case with MANGBUTU-EFE. [...] In all languages there are Tone Classes in Nouns and Verbs. 2b. Stress. Larochette reports a tendency towards stress on the penultimate syllable of a word or phrase in MANGBETU, accompanied sometimes by extra high tone as in nɛkâ-ˈkídriɔ, headache. No such uniformity of stress pattern, however, has been found in the other Language Groups. Even such intimately closely allied languages as MORU and MA'DI have quite different stress behaviour.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (empty rule) and the existing Vorbichler 1967 statement 'tone language, no stress statement': Tucker & Bryan give three (apparent) tone levels for Mangbutu-Efe and no stress placement for Mamvu. Vorbichler's review (p. 452) refines Tucker & Bryan by asserting 'irrefutable proof' of three tonemes in Mamvu where Tucker & Bryan only say it 'would seem to be the case'; his penultimate-stress remark concerns Balese (Lese), not Mamvu.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mamvu (the chapter's 'main exponent' of the MANGBUTU-EFE group) is treated as a tone language with apparently three tone levels and tone classes in nouns and verbs; the Stress section gives no placement for Mamvu or any Mangbutu-Efe language, saying only that the penultimate tendency reported for Mangbetu has no counterpart ('No such uniformity of stress pattern.. has been found in the other Language Groups'). The only concrete stress rules on the page are for Moru (first syllable of disyllables) and Ma'di (final vowel), not for Mamvu. Full-text probes of the whole book (archive.org FTS and Open Library search-inside: MAMVU/MANGBUTU-EFE/LESE/EFE with stress, stressed, unstressed, accent, prominence, penultimate, first/final syllable, length) surface no sentence predicating stress of Mamvu.
new_statements.exceptions: none for Mamvu; the chapter notes 'Tone Classes in MANGBUTU-EFE have yet to be worked out' (scanned snippet), i.e. the tonal analysis of the group is provisional
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's chapter treats MANGBUTU-EFE as a group with MAMVU 'chosen here as main exponent' (chapter head, c. p. 27); the stress paragraph's negative statement is group-level ('the other Language Groups'), not Mamvu-specific. The Mamvu forms in the Word Shape tables (p. 32: kàdru tongue, kárí bird, kɔ̀sà navel, káɓɔ́ fowl, ùɓɔ̀ village, bàŋgú breast) are from Tucker's own field notes with London informants; no dialect is named.
